To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the structure of the E. coli population was conserved among buffalo and cattle in the southern part Hwange ecosystem; (ii) antibiotic resistance genes were detected in the E. coli populations of buffalo and cattle in contact, suggesting the role of the interface in the dissemination process; and (iii) the study of antibiotic resistance at the wildlife/animal interface is a key element to better understand the dissemination of resistance in multihost systems.
the human/animal/wildlife interface can facilitate the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes and bacteria between hosts.

In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the risk of bacterial resistance dissemination between hosts, in a context of increasing human/animal contact.
the study of the E. coli population structure and antibiotic resistance at a buffalo/cattle interface.
the identification of the potential risks associated with bacterial resistance dissemination in a multihost system at an interface between human, livestock, and wildlife.

the human/cattle/buffalo interface in the southern part Hwange ecosystem is a potential reservoir for antibiotic resistance dissemination.
the human/animal/wildlife interface is a potential reservoir of antibiotic resistance dissemination.

antibiotic resistance is not a random phenomenon and that the human/animal contact is a potential source of resistance dissemination in wildlife populations.

the study of antibiotic resistance in multihost systems, and in particular at human/animal interface, is essential to understand and mitigate its threats.
